title: Working with Classes and Instances
objective: Give an attribute a default value in __init__(), then update it both directly and through a method.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose, examples, and exercises are original Code Forge material using an original theme, not the book's example classes.

paragraphs: Not every attribute needs to come from an argument. Inside __init__(), you can also assign a fixed starting value directly, giving every new instance the same default state before anything else happens to it.

Once an instance exists, you can change its attributes in two ways. The direct way reaches straight into the instance with dot notation, such as instance.attribute = new_value. This works, but it bypasses whatever logic the class might otherwise run.

The second way is to call a method that updates the attribute on the instance's behalf. A method can print a message, check the new value, or update more than one attribute at once — plain direct assignment cannot do any of that.
explanation.rule: Give an attribute a default value inside __init__(), then update it either directly with dot notation or through a method that changes it for you.

examples.title: A Default Value, Then Two Ways to Change It
examples.code:
class Torch:
    """A torch that starts out unlit."""

    def __init__(self, fuel_type):
        self.fuel_type = fuel_type
        self.is_lit = False  # Every torch starts unlit by default.

    def light(self):
        self.is_lit = True
        print("The torch flares to life.")


camp_torch = Torch("oil")
print(camp_torch.is_lit)

camp_torch.is_lit = True  # Change the attribute directly.
print(camp_torch.is_lit)

camp_torch.is_lit = False
camp_torch.light()  # Change the attribute through a method instead.
print(camp_torch.is_lit)
examples.note: fuel_type comes from an argument, but is_lit gets a default value of False right inside __init__(). The example then changes is_lit both directly with dot notation and indirectly by calling light().

checks.question: Which statement changes an attribute directly, without going through a method?

feedback.correct: Correct — dot notation followed by = reaches straight into the instance without calling any method.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Look for the line that assigns straight to an attribute with dot notation instead of calling a method.

assignment.title: Training Dummy
assignment.brief: Write a TrainingDummy class whose hit count starts at zero, then change it directly and through a method.
requirements: Implement __init__(self, name) that stores name as self.name and gives self.hit_count a default value of 0.
Implement a method record_hit() that increases self.hit_count by 1 and prints f"{self.name} has been hit {self.hit_count} time(s)."
Create a TrainingDummy instance, set its hit_count directly to 5 using dot notation, then call record_hit() once.
assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----
import io, contextlib
_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):
    _cf_dummy = TrainingDummy("Straw Man")
    _cf_dummy.hit_count = 2
    _cf_dummy.record_hit()
    _cf_dummy.record_hit()
_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()
print("__CF_TEST_OUTPUT__")
print(repr(_cf_result))
assignment.expectedOutput:
Straw Man has been hit 3 time(s).
Straw Man has been hit 4 time(s).
assignment.outputCheckLabel: Two record_hit() calls after setting hit_count = 2 print counts 3 then 4

hints: Inside __init__(self, name), set self.hit_count = 0 so every dummy starts at zero without needing an argument for it.
record_hit() should add 1 to self.hit_count before it prints anything.
Use an f-string in record_hit() so the message always shows the current self.hit_count.
After creating the instance, set dummy.hit_count = 5 directly with dot notation, then call dummy.record_hit() once.
